The Panama Canal expansion added a third lane of larger locks to the Panama Canal, one set on the Atlantic side and one on the Pacific. Work began in 2007, after Panamanians approved it in a referendum in 2006, and the new locks opened on 26 June 2016.

The old locks, finished in 1914, fixed the size of ocean ships for a century: the Panamax standard. By the 2000s many container ships were too big for them. The new locks take New Panamax ships, about one and a half times as large, which carry more than twice the cargo. The project also deepened and widened the channels. To save fresh water, each new lock has side basins that reuse part of the water from every filling.

It was the biggest change to the canal since it opened, and the first carried out under Panama's own control, which began in 1999 under the Torrijos-Carter Treaties. Ports on the east coast of the United States dredged their harbours to take the bigger ships. A drought in 2023 later forced the canal to cut traffic, a sign of how much it depends on rain.
